summary:
Maryland prohibits discrimination based on gender identity across the state under the Fairness for All Marylanders Act of 2014, effective 1 October 2014, covering employment, housing and public accommodations. Before that date, coverage existed only in Baltimore City, Baltimore County, Howard County, Hyattsville and Montgomery County.

The state hate-crime law adds penalties for crimes motivated by actual or perceived gender identity, and a 2021 amendment effective 1 October 2021 listed gender identity as a separate category. The common-law gay or trans panic defence was abolished by HB231, also effective 1 October 2021.

Maryland declared itself a sanctuary jurisdiction for protecting and defending transgender individuals through legislation passed 33-13 in the Senate and 97-38 in the House, signed by Governor Wes Moore and effective 1 October 2024. It followed a June 2023 executive order protecting unimpeded access to gender-affirming healthcare and an insurance law effective 1 January 2024.

State identity documents are comparatively open. A birth-certificate gender-marker change has been available since 1 October 2015 without surgery or sterilisation, on certification from a licensed healthcare provider confirming gender identity. The X marker remains unavailable on Maryland birth certificates as of 2023, while Motor Vehicle Administration identification cards and voter registration have allowed X since 1 October 2019 without legal or medical documentation. HB39, effective 1 October 2021, repealed the requirement to publish a legal name change in a newspaper before it is recorded on a birth certificate. The University of Maryland states it will add X in 2026.

Facilities access is protected by litigation and ordinance. In March 2018 a federal court ruled that transgender students may use restrooms and locker rooms aligned with their gender identity, striking down a Talbot County policy. Montgomery County adopted gender-neutral bathrooms by a 9-0 vote in July 2022 and Baltimore provides them by ordinance. A February 2022 county report records that transgender athletes may participate according to gender identity without proof, documentation or medical and legal transition, after 2022-2023 bills to restrict teams by biological sex failed.

Violence against trans residents is documented. On 11 September 2026 Sophie Lee, a 27-year-old Black trans woman, was found shot in Baltimore's Charles Village and died. A report of 13 September 2026 records her as the second Black trans woman shot to death in Baltimore within ten weeks.

Care access rests on state funding decisions. Medicaid explicitly covers sexual reassignment surgery for eligible residents over 18 under a bill passed in March 2023, signed in April 2023 and effective 1 January 2024. The Trans Health Equity Act, sponsored by Del. Anne Kaiser, D-Montgomery, passed the Maryland House of Delegates as of 20 May 2024 to extend Medicaid coverage of gender-affirming treatment; its path runs through the Maryland Senate and its current status is unresolved in the sources.

Maryland has recognised same-sex marriage since 1 January 2013 under the Civil Marriage Protection Act, so a trans visitor in a relationship that would be locally read as same-sex enters a jurisdiction where that marriage is valid.
tangentialFactors:
A July 2026 analysis by The Needle plots recorded anti-trans incidents against each state's law score. Maryland sits in the "Safest States" band with a law score of 23.5 and 11.1 recorded incidents, while Louisiana records both the worst law score at 24.7 and the highest recorded count at 11.6. The analysis's finding is that protective law floors do not by themselves predict incident counts.

Both figures are raw counts, and the source supplies no per-capita or population denominator, so the ordering cannot be read as a measure of risk per person. Maryland's 11.1 and Louisiana's 11.6 are close in absolute terms, and a populous state's raw count is expected to exceed a small state's regardless of conditions on the ground.

The protections described here govern Maryland's own institutions and courts. They do not determine how travel documents or entry screening are handled at federal level, which sits outside this state-level assessment.
localsOnly:
Residents are covered in employment, housing and public accommodations by the 2014 gender-identity statute and, in the same settings, by sexual-orientation protection in force since the Antidiscrimination Act of 2001.

Conversion therapy by licensed practitioners on minors has been banned since 1 October 2018, and a federal constitutional challenge to the ban was dismissed in September 2019.

Protection machinery includes Montgomery County's unanimous October 2020 LGBTIQ+ bill of rights ordinance, a Commission on LGBTIQ+ Affairs established by HB130 effective October 2021 with 15 members and expanded to 21 members in April 2023, and HB1380 effective 1 October 2022 restoring honourable discharges retrospectively to LGBT individuals who lived in Maryland at the time.

Medicaid covers sexual reassignment surgery for eligible residents over 18, and a legal name change no longer requires newspaper publication. Gender-neutral bathrooms operate by ordinance in Montgomery County and Baltimore.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Maryland-specific prison placement rule, special unit or named case for transgender prisoners is documented in the sources reviewed. National custody policy material covering the 2015 to 2018 period contains no Maryland-specific content, so the placement a trans resident would actually face in a Maryland facility is unresolved here.

The Trans Health Equity Act's status in the Maryland Senate is unresolved. The sources record only its passage in the House of Delegates as of 20 May 2024 and note that its path runs through the Senate.

The unavailability of X on Maryland birth certificates is stated as of 2023 and may since have changed. The University of Maryland's addition of X in 2026 is a stated plan rather than a confirmed fact.

The incident figures come from a single July 2026 analysis with no per-capita denominator, and the sources give no Maryland-specific count of anti-trans homicides beyond the two Baltimore cases reported in September 2026.
